analysis.one_liner: Pilots government-guaranteed jobs with living wages and benefits in high-unemployment communities.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: after its February 2026 introduction it was sent to two House committees, and neither has held a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a small federal pilot to test the idea of a federal job guarantee. The Labor Department would award competitive grants to up to 15 local governments, tribal entities, or groups of them — but only in areas where unemployment is at least 150 percent of the national rate. Those areas would have to offer a job to anyone 18 or older who applies, paying at least the prevailing wage for similar work, with health coverage comparable to federal employees' insurance and paid family and sick leave. Workers could not displace existing employees, and the jobs would be folded into existing union bargaining units where they exist. Federal agencies could also offer jobs at the pilot sites, and employers would get an existing tax credit (the Work Opportunity Tax Credit) for hiring people out of the program.
analysis.who_benefits: People in high-unemployment communities — including tribal areas — who want a job and can't find one would get guaranteed employment at the prevailing or local wage, with federal-employee-grade health coverage, paid family and sick leave, and supportive services like child care, transportation, and housing help. The bill directs job priorities toward child care, care for seniors and people with disabilities, clean energy, and sustainable infrastructure. Areas with high poverty, former prisoners reentering the workforce, and people with employment barriers are singled out for access and training support.

how_it_helps.text: Any adult 18 or older living in a participating high-unemployment area who applies gets a job, at a wage that must be the greater of the local required wage, the prevailing wage for similar work, or an applicable union contract rate [S2].

Participants get health insurance comparable to the Federal Employee Health Benefits Program, plus paid family leave and paid sick leave, and can use grant funds for child care, transportation, housing, training, literacy programs, and reentry help for people with criminal records [S2].

Jobs must join existing bargaining units and are covered by any applicable collective bargaining agreement, and grant funds cannot be used to displace existing workers or break existing contracts [S2].
Federal agencies would make jobs available at the pilot sites, and employers would receive the Work Opportunity Tax Credit for hiring anyone who spent at least three months in the program [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill writes a blank check: it appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' from the Treasury with no dollar cap, deposited into a new Job Guarantee Program Trust Fund. There is no cost estimate attached to the bill. Local governments in pilot areas may also chip in.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates unlimited federal money ('such sums as may be necessary') for the program without stating a cost, and no cost estimate from the Congressional Budget Office is attached to the bill as introduced [S2].

The wage and leave provisions are tied to bills from the previous Congress — a $15-plus minimum wage bill (S. 2488), a paid leave bill (S. 1714), and a paid sick leave bill (S. 1664) — that never became law, so the floor is 'if enacted' and may not exist; wages default to local and prevailing-wage rules [S2].
The pilot is small and short: grants run at most three years, only 15 sites are funded, and funding ends with the grant, so the bill tests but does not deliver a permanent guarantee [S2].
Expanding the Work Opportunity Tax Credit to program participants gives private employers a federal tax subsidy for hiring these workers, routing public money through private payrolls [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a guaranteed public job can be expensive per participant and that design questions — what the jobs are, how they interact with existing benefits programs — are exactly what a pilot is meant to answer before scaling up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who would be served at the up-to-15 pilot sites, the direct benefits are substantial and concrete: a real job at a prevailing wage, union protections, decent health coverage, and paid leave. The bill is honest about being a pilot — capped sites, three years, rigorous evaluation required — which limits both its cost and its reach. The open-ended appropriation is the main design weakness; a skeptic would want a firm dollar figure before Congress commits to it. On balance it is a measured test of a large idea rather than the large idea itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees, and as of now neither committee has taken it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Federal Jobs Guarantee Development Act of 2026 on February 12, 2026, joined by three Democratic cosponsors — Reps. Ilhan Omar, Summer Lee of Pennsylvania, and LaMonica McIver [S2].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Education and Workforce Committee and to the Ways and Means Committee, with the Speaker to determine which committee handles which parts [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].
The bill has no Republican cosponsors — all four listed cosponsors are Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody changed position: the job guarantee remains untested, federal money was never spent, and the communities the bill was written for are no better off than before it was introduced. Federal taxpayers are spared an open-ended new spending commitment, and private employers in pilot areas never faced competition for workers from a guaranteed public job.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one moved; the status quo held

for.name: Reps. Ilhan Omar, Summer Lee, and LaMonica McIver
for.role: Original cosponsors (3 of the bill's 4 cosponsors)

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in February 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral (has jurisdiction over the bill's tax credit provision)
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral for the tax provisions; no action has been taken.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Democrat — five members total, no Republicans — and no committee action has followed the referral.

industries.industry: Local governments and tribal entities in high-unemployment areas
industries.note: They would receive federal grants to run job guarantee programs and could add state, local, or philanthropic funds. The jobs created — child care, elder care, clean energy, infrastructure — would be public and community-serving rather than profit-making.

industries.industry: Private employers (via the Work Opportunity Tax Credit)
industries.note: Employers would get a federal tax credit for hiring anyone who spent three months in the job guarantee program. The credit reduces what those employers owe in taxes, paid for by the Treasury.

industries.industry: Low-wage and staffing employers in pilot areas
industries.note: A guaranteed public job at prevailing wage, with health coverage and paid leave, would give workers in those areas an alternative to the lowest-paying jobs, tightening the labor market for employers who compete for the same workers. The bill forbids displacing existing employees, so the effect runs through worker choice rather than layoffs.
Agencies would be asked to make jobs available at pilot sites, reimbursed in full from the trust fund, adding participants and some administrative work but no net cost to their budgets.

analysis.trajectory: With only five cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action more than a year into the session, the bill's realistic path is the same one most bills take: it sits in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 and never receives a vote. Its best realistic outcome within this session is a hearing or a cost estimate, not floor action.
